topics.title: Visit of Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan to Sri Lanka

subtopics.title: Bilateral Ties and Cooperation Areas
subtopics.summary: Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan made the first-ever bilateral visit to Sri Lanka and held talks with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in Colombo. The visit highlighted trade, development, defence and development-linked cooperation between India and Sri Lanka. India is Sri Lanka's largest trade partner and largest source of tourists.

Sri Lanka joins the International Big Cat Alliance

subtopics.title: Diaspora Schemes: PIO and OCI
subtopics.summary: The OCI scheme was introduced in 2005 through an amendment to the Citizenship Act, 1955, and was merged with the PIO scheme in 2015. PIO card holders need no visa to visit India for 15 years from the date of issue of the card. OCI holders get a multipurpose, multiple-entry, lifelong visa and are exempt from police reporting.

subtopics.title: Katchatheevu Island Dispute
subtopics.summary: Katchatheevu is an uninhabited 285-acre island in the Palk Strait, and its ownership remained disputed until 1974. Sri Lanka based its claim on early medieval rule and Portuguese jurisdiction, while India's claim traced control through the Ramnad Zamindari under the Nayak dynasty of Madurai. Tensions over Indian fishermen after the 2009 Sri Lanka Civil War have renewed demands over the island.
facts: Katchatheevu is an uninhabited 285-acre island located in the Palk Strait
The island was once part of the Madras Presidency
Ownership remained a point of dispute between India and Sri Lanka until 1974
Sri Lanka's claim: Jaffna Kingdom ruled the island in the early medieval period
Sri Lanka's claim: Portuguese (1505-1658 CE) exercised jurisdiction over the islet
India's claim: control later shifted to the Ramnad Zamindari under the Nayak dynasty of Madurai in the 17th century
Indo-Sri Lankan Maritime Agreement 1974, under Indira Gandhi, agreed to cede the island to Sri Lanka
The 1974 agreement allowed Indian fishermen continued access to Katchatheevu
Additional Agreement of 1976 barred fishing by both countries in each other's EEZ, with the island at the boundary

subtopics.title: Sri Lanka Profile and Strategic Context
subtopics.summary: Colombo is the executive capital of Sri Lanka and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte houses the legislature, with Harini Amarasuriya as Prime Minister and Anura Kumara Dissanayake as President. The LTTE, formed in 1976, and the 13th Amendment shape Sri Lanka's internal politics. China's growing presence through financial aid and Hambantota Port raises strategic concerns for India.

PM: Harini Amarasuriya; President: Anura Kumara Dissanayake
Currency: Sri Lankan Rupee
LTTE was formed in 1976 as a self-styled 'National Freedom Movement of People of Tamil Eelam'
LTTE undertook terrorist activities in Sri Lanka, especially against Sinhalese

subtopics.title: Bill and Lok Sabha expansion
subtopics.summary: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was proposed along with the Delimitation Bill, 2026 to restructure representation. It would expand the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 seats, with 815 for States and 35 for Union Territories. Seat allocation and delimitation would use the 2011 Census, and Parliament would decide which population data to use.
facts: Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 proposed with the Delimitation Bill, 2026
Lok Sabha to expand from 543 to 850 seats
Proposed 850 seats: 815 for States and 35 for Union Territories
Current Lok Sabha strength: 543 elected members
2011 Census used for seat allocation and delimitation
Article 82 amended to lift the freeze on redrawing constituency boundaries
Parliament empowered to decide which population data to use
Current Lok Sabha seat freeze is based on the 1971 Census under the 84th Amendment

subtopics.title: Women's reservation
subtopics.summary: The Bill overrides the delay linked to the Census for women's reservation under the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam. Reservation is for one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, valid for 15 years and extendable by Parliament. Reserved constituencies rotate after each delimitation, and the reservation does not extend to the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils.
facts: Women's Reservation Act, 2023 is the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act
One-third of total seats in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies reserved for women
Article 330A: reservation for women in the Lok Sabha
Article 332A: reservation for women in State Legislative Assemblies
Article 239AA: reservation for women in the NCT of Delhi
Article 334A: reservation effective after delimitation and Census
Reservation valid for 15 years and can be extended
Reserved seats rotate after each delimitation
Within SC/ST reserved seats, one-third reserved for SC/ST women under the Bill
Women's reservation bills were introduced in 1996, 1998, 2009, 2010 and 2014
No women's reservation in the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils

subtopics.title: Delimitation and the Commission
subtopics.summary: Delimitation redraws territorial constituency boundaries so that representation stays fair after population changes. Article 82 requires Parliament to pass a Delimitation Act after every Census, and the President appoints the Delimitation Commission. The Delimitation Bill, 2026 gives the Commission civil court powers and states that its orders cannot be challenged in courts.
facts: Delimitation defines territorial constituency boundaries after population changes
Article 82: Parliament to pass a Delimitation Act after every Census
Article 170 governs the division of constituencies for State Assemblies
President appoints the Delimitation Commission in consultation with the Election Commission
Commission members: a retired Supreme Court judge (Chairperson), the Chief Election Commissioner and State Election Commissioners
Commission decisions are final and not subject to court review or modification by Parliament or State Assemblies
Delimitation Commissions were formed under Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002
No Commission was formed after the 1981 and 1991 Censuses
84th Amendment (2002) extended the freeze until the first Census after 2026

subtopics.title: Concerns and consequences
subtopics.summary: Critics point to federal imbalance, with the South's share of Lok Sabha seats projected to fall from 24.3% to about 20.7%. Concerns also include outdated 2011 data, removal of judicial review and excess legislative control over delimitation. Supporters point to smaller constituencies, better grievance redressal and a more efficient use of MPLADS funds.
facts: Federal imbalance: Southern States' share falls from 24.3% to about 20.7%
Northern dominance: high population growth states gain more seats
Outdated data: the 2011 Census may distort representation for decades
Judicial review removed: risk of gerrymandering
Excess legislative control: Parliament's discretion may politicise delimitation
Ministers capped at 15% of Lok Sabha strength under Article 75(1A)
Joint sittings: Lok Sabha dominance dilutes the Rajya Sabha's federal role
Expansion reduces constituency size and improves accessibility and grievance redressal
Census dependency delays implementation of women's reservation

topics.title: World's Largest Digital Census Begins: Census 2027 (Phase 1)

subtopics.title: Census 2027 Phase I and digital enumeration
subtopics.summary: India has launched Phase I of Census 2027, described as the world's largest population count and the first fully digital enumeration exercise. Phase I is a House Listing and Housing Census, with self-enumeration from 1 April 2026 and a field exercise from 16 April to 15 May 2026 in notified States and UTs. The exercise relies on mobile applications, web-based data collection and digital mapping tools.
facts: Phase I of Census 2027 is a House Listing and Housing Census.
Self-enumeration began on 1 April 2026.
Field exercise runs from 16 April to 15 May 2026 in notified States and UTs.
Key focus areas: housing conditions, household amenities, assets and infrastructure.
Described as the first fully digital census exercise in India.
Digital tools: mobile applications, web-based data collection and digital mapping tools.
Self-enumeration works through a secure web portal and is available in 16 languages.
Stated limitation: only residents currently present in India are covered.
The Census 2027 questionnaire contains 33 questions.

subtopics.title: Census history and caste enumeration
subtopics.summary: Population counts are traced to the Arthashastra, Ain-e-Akbari and Rig Veda. The modern census developed in the colonial period, with a non-synchronous national census in 1871 and a synchronous census in 1881. The 1931 census was the last caste-based census, and after Independence only SC and ST data has been collected.
facts: Ancient references to population counts appear in the Arthashastra, Ain-e-Akbari and Rig Veda.
The 1871 national census was non-synchronous and was conducted under Lord Mayo.
The 1881 synchronous census was conducted by WC Plowden under Lord Rippon.
JH Hutton was Census Commissioner in 1931; RA Gopalaswami was Census Commissioner in 1951.
The 1931 census was the last caste-based census.
After 1947 only SC and ST data was collected; OBCs have been excluded until now.
The 1921 census is the only census to witness a decadal population decline.
Bihar, Karnataka and Telangana undertook independent caste surveys, in that order.
India has held 7 censuses since Independence.

subtopics.title: Constitutional and legal framework
subtopics.summary: The Union's power to conduct the census rests on Article 246 and Entry 69 of the Union List. The Census Act, 1948 provides the legal mandate and makes participation mandatory. The 84th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 froze Lok Sabha seat allocation on 1971 Census data until the first census conducted after 2026.
facts: The Union has the power to conduct the census under Article 246 and Entry 69 of the Union List.
Articles 81 and 82 relate to Lok Sabha seat distribution and delimitation after 2026.
The 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 froze Lok Sabha seat allocation using 1971 Census data.
The freeze lasts until the first census conducted after 2026.
The Census Act, 1948 provides the legal mandate and makes participation mandatory.
The census is managed by the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India, Mritunjay Kumar Narayan.

subtopics.title: Purpose of the census and its challenges
subtopics.summary: Census data supports delimitation, women's one-third seat reservation and planning for healthcare, education and infrastructure. Unlike sample surveys, the census offers comprehensive population data. Challenges include limited rural digital access, caste data inconsistencies, logistics, public trust and administrative capacity.
facts: Caste data is seen as key to sharpen welfare schemes such as PM Awas Yojana and Skill India.
Caste data aids delimitation and enables Women's One-Third Seat Reservation in Parliament and Assemblies.
Unlike sample surveys, the census offers comprehensive population data.
Demographic data is vital for planning healthcare, education and infrastructure.
Census forms are the basis for updating the National Population Register.
Challenge: limited rural access to digital tools.
Challenge: avoid duplication and inconsistencies in caste data.
Challenge: large-scale training and coverage of remote areas.
Challenge: public trust, given fears around NPR/NRC linkages.
Challenge: administrative capacity, covering funds, staffing and inter-agency coordination.

subtopics.title: NPR, CAA and NRC compared
subtopics.summary: The NPR is a nationwide database of every resident, including foreigners, meant for government schemes. The CAA covers minority refugees from Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh who came to India before 31 December 2014. The NRC covers citizens of India with valid identity documents, and only Assam currently updates it.
facts: NPR is a database of every resident, including foreigners.
NPR covers residents who have lived at an address for the last 6 months and will stay there for the next 6 months.
NPR is meant to be used for government schemes and has nationwide coverage.
CAA covers minority refugees (Hindu, Christian, Sikh, Parsi, Jain, Buddhist) from Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh.
CAA covers those minority refugees who came to India before 31 December 2014.
NRC covers citizens of India with valid identity documents.
Currently, only Assam updates the NRC.
Government's answer: there is no duplication between NPR and Aadhaar, as the objectives are different.
Government's answer: Muslims are not a minority in the 3 neighbouring countries, so they are not mentioned.

subtopics.title: Origins, Ideology and Causes of LWE
subtopics.summary: Left Wing Extremism (LWE) traces back to a 1967 uprising in Naxalbari, West Bengal, and aims at societal and political change through revolutionary methods. Its ideology seeks to overthrow the central government through armed revolution and to set up a communist state based on Maoist principles. The booklet links the movement's growth to tribal displacement, tribal resentment over forest laws, poverty and weak governance.
facts: Originated in the 1967 uprising in Naxalbari, West Bengal
Aim: societal and political change through revolutionary methods
Ideology: overthrow the central government through armed revolution
Methods include violence and guerrilla warfare
Goal: establish a communist state based on Maoist principles
Massive displacement of tribal population due to development projects and mining operations
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 prohibits tribes from harvesting forest resources
Poverty and lack of sustainable means drive people to join the Naxalite movement
Lack of effective governance is a listed factor responsible for the movement
Insufficient technical intelligence against Naxalism is a listed factor responsible for the movement

subtopics.title: Current LWE Landscape and Factors Behind the Decline
subtopics.summary: The booklet reports a sharp fall in LWE-affected districts, from 126 in 2014 to about 7 in 2026, with the remaining hotspots in Chhattisgarh. Violence fell as well, with incidents down 88% and deaths down 90% between 2010 and 2025. The measures credited for this include tactical operations, road and mobile connectivity, action against funding networks, surrender incentives and administrative expansion.
facts: LWE-affected districts reduced from 126 (2014) to about 7 (2026)
Residual hotspots: Bijapur, Sukma and Narayanpur in Chhattisgarh
Incidents of violence down 88%: 1,936 in 2010 to 234 in 2025
Deaths down 90%: 1,005 in 2010
Red Corridor: severe Naxalism-Maoist insurgency across ten listed states, including Kerala and Telangana
Tactical dominance by COBRA and Greyhounds, using company operating bases to penetrate remote zones
Infrastructure integration: 12,000 km of all-weather roads reduced geographical isolation of insurgents
Information warfare: 9,000+ mobile (4G) towers countered Maoist propaganda and integrated tribal regions digitally
Financial crackdown: NIA and Enforcement Directorate action and asset seizures disrupted urban funding networks
Surrender-cum-Rehabilitation Policy: 10,000+ cadres surrendered since 2014, with cash benefits and skill training

subtopics.title: Government Initiatives: Policy, SAMADHAN and Tribal Development
subtopics.summary: The government's response combines a 2015 national policy and action plan with the SAMADHAN doctrine, a set of eight elements running from leadership to financing. Parallel development schemes target tribal regions, including the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan and PM-JANMAN. The booklet also cites the 2006 Bandyopadhyay Committee, which highlighted governance and discrimination gaps faced by tribals.
facts: National Policy and Action Plan to address Left Wing Extremism, 2015
SAMADHAN doctrine: Smart leadership, Aggressive strategy, Motivation and training, Actionable intelligence
SAMADHAN also covers Dashboard based KPIs and KRAs, Harnessing technology, Action plan for each theatre and No access to financing
Special Central Assistance (SCA) supports public infrastructure and services

topics.title: Gujarat Passed Uniform Civil Code Bill 2026

subtopics.title: Key Features of Gujarat UCC
subtopics.summary: Gujarat passed the Uniform Civil Code Bill 2026, becoming the second state after Uttarakhand to enact a UCC. The Bill creates a uniform civil framework that replaces diverse religious personal laws on marriage, divorce and inheritance. It also sets registration deadlines, bans polygamy and bigamy, and routes separations through civil courts.
facts: Gujarat is the second state to enact a UCC, after Uttarakhand.
Uniform civil framework replaces diverse religious personal laws on marriage, divorce and inheritance.
Gender equality: equal inheritance rights for sons and daughters.
Marriage must be registered within 60 days.
Live-in relationships must be registered within 30 days.
Monogamy rule prohibits polygamy and bigamy.
All separations must be processed through civil courts (judicial exclusivity in divorce).
Scheduled Tribes are excluded to preserve their customary practices and cultural identity.

subtopics.title: Background and Constitutional Basis
subtopics.summary: The need for a uniform law was first considered in the Lex Loci Report of 1840, and the colonial government formed the B N Rau Committee in 1941 to examine common Hindu laws. Article 44 urges the state to establish a UCC, but it is part of the non-enforceable DPSP. Personal laws on marriage, divorce and succession sit in the Concurrent List, so both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate on them.
facts: Lex Loci Report of 1840 first considered the need for a uniform law.
Colonial government formed the B N Rau Committee in 1941.
B N Rau Committee examined the necessity of common Hindu laws and recommended a codified Hindu law giving equal rights to women.
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 codified intestate succession among Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs.
Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was chosen by Nehru in 1948 to chair the sub-committee developing the Hindu Code Bill.
Four Hindu Code Bills: Hindu Marriage Act 1955; Hindu Succession, Hindu Minority and Guardianship, and Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Acts 1956.
Underlying principle of UCC: laws should be gender-neutral and religion-neutral.
Article 44 urges the state to establish a uniform civil code; it is part of the DPSP and is not enforceable.
Personal laws on marriage, divorce and succession are under the Concurrent List.

subtopics.title: Views, Courts and Landmark Cases
subtopics.summary: Views on UCC differ across the Law Commissions, the Central Government, the Constitution's framers and the Supreme Court. The 21st Law Commission found a UCC neither necessary nor desirable in 2018, while the Central Government favours one. Landmark judgments such as Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, Shayara Bano and Jose Paulo Coutinho have shaped the debate.
facts: 21st Law Commission (2018) found a UCC neither necessary nor desirable at this stage and recommended reforming family laws across religions.
Framers of the Constitution did not intend total uniformity and placed personal laws in the Concurrent List.
Central Government favours a UCC and calls different property and matrimonial laws a threat to national unity.
Supreme Court has called for implementing the UCC in many cases.
Shah Bano Begum case (1985): maintenance under Section 125 CrPC even after the iddat period.
Sarla Mudgal case (1995): a Hindu husband cannot convert to Islam and remarry without dissolving his first marriage.
Shayara Bano case (2017): triple talaq declared unconstitutional; Parliament urged to regulate Muslim marriages and divorces.
Indian Young Lawyers Association case (2018): personal and customary law falls under Article 13.
Jose Paulo Coutinho case (2019): Goa hailed as a 'shining example' of a UCC.
22nd Law Commission issued a notification seeking views on UCC.

subtopics.title: Arguments For and Against the UCC
subtopics.summary: The UCC is presented as a way to promote gender equality, eliminate discriminatory practices against women, align with India's secular nature and reform outdated, regressive practices. Critics argue that it conflicts with the right to freedom of religion under Articles 25-28, that some civil laws are inseparably linked to religious beliefs, and that it could be politically exploited and lead to social unrest.
facts: Objective: promote gender equality.
Objective: eliminate discriminatory practices against women.
Objective: align with the secular nature of the Indian state.
Objective: reform outdated and regressive practices.
Concern: UCC is seen as against the right to freedom of religion guaranteed under Articles 25-28.
Concern: some civil laws are inseparably connected with religious beliefs and practices.
Concern: implementation could be politically exploited, leading to social unrest.
Concern: a UCC might not accommodate the unique customs and sensitivities of different communities.

subtopics.title: Dispute background and positions
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi dispute concerns how the river's waters are shared between upstream Chhattisgarh and downstream Odisha. Odisha says upstream construction has reduced its downstream flow, while Chhattisgarh cites its larger catchment share and development needs. The conflict is sharpest in the non-monsoon season and is intensified by the absence of a formal sharing agreement.
facts: Dispute escalated around 2016 after increased upstream infrastructure development
Odisha approached the Supreme Court of India, which led to a tribunal being constituted
Odisha argues that upstream constructions by Chhattisgarh reduced downstream water flow
Odisha's concerns: irrigation, drinking water supply, fisheries and ecological sustainability
Chhattisgarh says it accounts for a larger share of the basin's catchment area
Chhattisgarh says its projects are necessary for regional development and water security
Dispute is most critical in the non-monsoon season when downstream water availability matters most
Absence of a formal inter-state water-sharing agreement has intensified the conflict

subtopics.title: Tribunal status and deadlock
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal has given both states a final opportunity to agree a water-sharing formula and has issued an ultimatum for a settlement by May 2. If no settlement is reached, the Tribunal will decide on available evidence and legal principles. The Tribunal has voiced dissatisfaction with repeated adjournments, and the deadlock is linked to unreliable data and a trust deficit.
facts: Tribunal granted both states a Final Opportunity to agree a mutually agreed water-sharing formula
Final ultimatum: present a water-sharing settlement to the Tribunal by May 2
If the states fail, the Tribunal will adjudicate on available evidence and legal principles
Tribunal will deliver a Final Judgment on Merits if Odisha and Chhattisgarh fail to settle
Tribunal is dissatisfied with repeated adjournments and lack of substantive progress
No concrete proposals or narrowing of contentious issues have been placed on record
Deadlock is attributed to absence of reliable and mutually accepted hydrological data
A persistent trust deficit between the two states has hindered negotiation and consensus

subtopics.title: Legal framework for inter-state waters
subtopics.summary: Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate inter-state river disputes and allows it to exclude courts' jurisdiction in such matters. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was used for the Mahanadi tribunal, and the River Boards Act, 1956 provides for river boards. Entries 17 and 56 divide powers between the States and the Union, and the Supreme Court cannot question a tribunal's award but can question its working.
facts: Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate disputes relating to inter-state rivers
Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate disputes relating to inter-State rivers
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was used to constitute the Mahanadi tribunal
Centre first tries consultation among aggrieved states; if that fails it may constitute a tribunal
River Boards Act, 1956 lets the Centre establish boards for inter-state rivers in consultation with states
A River Board is to meet at least thrice a year and the Prime Minister is its Chairman
No River Board has been created to date
Entry 17 (State List) covers water supplies, irrigation, canals, drainage and embankments
Entry 56 (Union List) empowers the Union to regulate and develop inter-state rivers in public interest
Supreme Court cannot question a tribunal's award or formula but can question its working

subtopics.title: River course and Hirakud Dam
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi originates at Sihawa Hill in Raipur, Chhattisgarh, and flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal. It receives left-bank and right-bank tributaries. Hirakud Dam on the river is described in the booklet as the longest earthen dam in the world.
facts: Mahanadi originates at Sihawa Hill in Raipur, Chhattisgarh
Mahanadi flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal
Left bank tributaries: Shivnath, Hasdeo, Mand and Ib
Right bank tributaries: Jonk, Ong and Tel
Hirakud Dam is the longest earthen dam in the world

subtopics.title: Other inter-state water tribunals
subtopics.summary: India has several inter-state water tribunals, each set up for a particular river dispute. The booklet lists tribunals formed between 1986 and 2018, covering states such as Punjab, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. The Mahanadi tribunal is one of these five.

Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal, formed 2010: Karnataka, Goa and Maharashtra
Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal, formed 2010: Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal, formed 2018: Chhattisgarh and Odisha

subtopics.title: Event details and key highlights
subtopics.summary: The 17th National Panchayati Raj Day was observed on 24 April at Vigyan Bhawan, organised by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. The theme was Sashakt Panchayat, Sarvangeen Vikas. The day marks the enforcement of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment and highlights initiatives such as the National Panchayat Awards and the Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0.

subtopics.title: Committees on Panchayati Raj (1957-1986)
subtopics.summary: Several committees shaped the idea of Panchayati Raj before it was given constitutional form. The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended democratic decentralisation, and Rajasthan became the first state to establish Panchayati Raj, at Nagaur, on 2 October 1959. Later committees under Ashok Mehta, G.V.K. Rao and L.M. Singhvi reviewed the system: the Ashok Mehta committee recommended a two-tier system, the G.V.K. Rao committee reviewed administrative arrangements for rural development and poverty alleviation programmes, and the Singhvi committee recommended constitutional recognition of panchayats.
facts: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) examined the Community Development Programme (1952) and the National Extension Service (1953).
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended democratic decentralisation, which came to be known as Panchayati Raj.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj system.
Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959 was the first state to establish Panchayati Raj.
Andhra Pradesh followed Rajasthan in adopting the system in 1959.
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977), appointed by the Janata Government, recommended a two-tier Panchayati Raj system.
The G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) reviewed administrative arrangements for Rural Development and Poverty Alleviation Programmes.
The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986), appointed by the Rajiv Gandhi Government, recommended that PRIs be constitutionally recognised, protected and preserved.
B.R. Mehta is known as the Father of Panchayati Raj and the Architect of Panchayati Raj.

subtopics.title: 73rd Constitutional Amendment: background and structure
subtopics.summary: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment bill was introduced in Lok Sabha in September 1991 by the Congress government under P V Narasimha Rao. It came into force on 24 April 1993 and added Part IX, The Panchayats, to the Constitution. The amendment also added an 11th Schedule and set a three-tier structure for panchayats in every State.
facts: The bill was introduced in Lok Sabha in September 1991 by the Congress government under P V Narasimha Rao.
The bill became the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
The Act came into force on 24 April 1993.
Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement the 73rd CAA.
A new Part IX, titled The Panchayats, covers Articles 243 to 243-O.
An 11th Schedule was added, containing 29 subjects of panchayats (Article 243-G).
Article 243-B provides for a three-tier system: village, intermediate and district levels.
A State with population not exceeding 20 lakh may not constitute panchayats at the intermediate level.
The amendment aims at governance closer to people, inclusive development, localised planning, digital transformation and transparency.

subtopics.title: Elections, reservation, term and oversight
subtopics.summary: All members of panchayats at each level are elected directly, while chairpersons at the intermediate and district levels are chosen indirectly. The amendment provides for reservation of seats for SCs, STs and women, and sets a five-year term with time limits for fresh elections. A State Election Commission supervises electoral rolls and elections, and a Finance Commission reviews panchayat finances.
facts: Article 243-C: all members of panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels are elected directly.
Chairpersons at intermediate and district levels are elected indirectly, by and from amongst the elected members.
The village-level chairperson is elected in the manner the State Legislature determines.
Article 243-D: seats are reserved for SCs and STs in proportion to their population.
Not less than one-third of total seats, and of chairperson offices, are reserved for women.
Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes is not applicable to Arunachal Pradesh.
Article 243-E: a panchayat has a five-year term but can be dissolved earlier.
Fresh elections must be completed before expiry of five years, or within six months of dissolution.
Article 243-K: a State Election Commission supervises electoral rolls and the conduct of panchayat elections; its State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor.
Article 243-I: the Governor constitutes a Finance Commission every five years to review panchayat finances.

subtopics.title: Exemptions, Union Territories and PESA
subtopics.summary: Some states and areas are exempted from Part IX, including Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram. Article 243-L lets the President extend Part IX to Union Territories with exceptions, and it applies there except Delhi. The PESA Act, 1996, enacted under Article 243-M, does not apply to Sixth Schedule areas.
facts: Under Article 243-M, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram are exempted.
Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas in the 5th and 6th Schedule states are exempted.
Hill Areas of Manipur for which District Councils exist are exempted.
The Darjeeling district of West Bengal, where the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists, is exempted.
Article 243-L: the President may direct that Part IX applies to a Union Territory, with exceptions and modifications.
Part IX applies to all Union Territories except Delhi.
The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, known as the PESA Act, was enacted under Article 243-M.
The PESA Act, 1996 is not applicable to Sixth Schedule areas.
The 6th Schedule states are Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

subtopics.title: Repo Rate and the Economy
subtopics.summary: The Repo Rate is the rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks, so changes to it ripple through borrowing and spending. A lower repo rate makes loans cheaper and supports growth, while a higher repo rate curbs excess spending and eases inflation. The RBI cut the rate by 25 basis points to 5.25% in December 2025.
facts: Repo stands for Repurchasing Option or Repurchase Agreement
Repo Rate: rate at which RBI lends money to commercial banks
Lower repo rate means cheaper loans for banks and lower interest rates for borrowers
Lower repo rate leads to increased borrowing and spending
Higher repo rate means costlier loans for banks and higher interest rates for consumers and businesses
RBI raises the Repo Rate during high levels of inflation to bring down the flow of money
Higher repo rate curbs excessive spending and slows investment and money supply
RBI lowers the Repo Rate when it needs to pump funds into the economy
Dec 2025: RBI cut Repo Rate by 25 basis points to 5.25%
Dec 2025 cut was the 4th reduction by RBI, totalling 125 basis points in 2025

subtopics.title: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)
subtopics.summary: The Monetary Policy Committee is a statutory body under the RBI Act, 1934 that sets the benchmark Repo Rate needed to keep inflation within the target. The Central Government constitutes it with six members, chaired ex-officio by the RBI Governor. It meets at least four times a year, decides by majority vote, and its decisions are binding on banks.
facts: Statutory body under the RBI Act, 1934
Responsible for setting the benchmark policy rate (Repo Rate)
Aim: contain inflation within the specified target level
Central Government is empowered to constitute a 6-member MPC
Ex-officio Chairperson: RBI Governor
Members: Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer nominated by Central Board, three members appointed by Central Government
Meets at least four times each year
Quorum: at least four members, including the RBI Governor or, in his absence, the Deputy Governor
Decisions are based on majority vote; in case of a tie the RBI Governor has the casting vote
MPC decisions are binding on banks

subtopics.title: Instruments of Monetary Policy
subtopics.summary: The RBI uses several instruments to manage liquidity, borrowing costs and the money supply. The Repo Rate and Reverse Repo Rate set the rates at which the RBI lends to and borrows from banks. Reserve requirements, the Bank Rate, the Marginal Standing Facility and open market operations each work through different channels. To tighten monetary policy, the RBI raises SLR.
facts: Repo Rate: rate at which RBI lends money to commercial banks
Reverse Repo Rate: rate at which RBI borrows money from commercial banks
SLR: statutory minimum percentage of deposits a bank must keep as liquid cash, gold or other securities
To tighten monetary policy, RBI will raise SLR
Marginal Standing Facility: window for banks to borrow overnight funds at a rate higher than the Repo Rate
Bank Rate: long-term rate (Repo is short-term) at which the central bank lends to other banks
An increase in Bank Rate increases interest rates on loans and deposits
CRR: banks must hold a proportion of their deposits as cash with the RBI
With an increase in CRR, banks increase their lending rates
Open Market Operations: purchase or sale of government securities to inject or absorb durable liquidity

subtopics.title: Inflation Targeting and the RBI
subtopics.summary: Inflation targeting means the central bank aims to keep inflation within a pre-defined range. India adopted flexible inflation targeting in 2016 with a 4% target and a deviation of plus or minus 2%. The RBI works to maintain price stability while promoting economic growth, and performs several roles in the financial system.
facts: Inflation targeting: monetary policy framework where the central bank aims to keep inflation within a targeted range
India adopted Flexible Inflation Targeting in 2016
India's inflation target is 4%, with a deviation of +/- 2%
Urjit Patel Committee (2014) formalised inflation targeting with a 4% target and 2% band
The 4% target and 2% band were first proposed by the Chakravarty Committee (1982-85)
Inflation target is set by the Government in consultation with RBI every 5 years, under the amended RBI Act, 1934
RBI aims to maintain price stability while promoting economic growth
RBI roles include monetary authority, lender of last resort, banker to government and custodian of forex reserves
Retail inflation is within the mandated target band of 2-6%
RBI was established on April 1 in Calcutta

subtopics.title: MC14 Deadlock and WTO Basics
subtopics.summary: The 14th WTO Ministerial Conference, held in Yaoundé (Cameroon), ended without consensus, reflecting a deep North-South divide. Pending issues were deferred to the WTO General Council meeting in Geneva. The WTO was established on 1 January 1995, and its Ministerial Conference is its highest decision-making body.
facts: MC14 was held in Yaoundé, Cameroon.
MC14 ended without consensus over the e-Commerce moratorium, agriculture and transparency norms.
The deadlock reflects a deep North-South divide.
Pending issues were deferred to the WTO General Council meeting in Geneva.
The WTO was established on 1 January 1995 under the 1994 Marrakesh Agreement.
The WTO is the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1948.
The Ministerial Conference is the WTO's highest decision-making body.
The Ministerial Conference meets at least once every two years.
The 13th Ministerial Conference was held in Abu Dhabi in 2024.

subtopics.title: E-Commerce Moratorium and Digital Trade
subtopics.summary: The WTO moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, in place since 1998, expired at MC14 for lack of consensus. Members are therefore theoretically free to impose taxes on digital goods and services. Meanwhile, a coalition of 66 members advanced talks on a plurilateral e-commerce agreement focused on data flows, digital transactions and consumer protection.
facts: The moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions has been in place since 1998.
The moratorium expired at MC14 due to lack of consensus.
Members cannot impose tariffs on electronic transmissions under the 1998 arrangement.
With the lapse, members are theoretically free to tax digital goods and services.
The moratorium covers software, music, films and digital services.
A coalition of 66 WTO members advanced negotiations on a plurilateral e-commerce agreement.
Focus areas of the plurilateral e-commerce agreement are data flows, digital transactions and consumer protection.
MC14 agenda included a decision on continuation of the moratorium on customs duties.

subtopics.title: Agriculture, Fisheries and Dispute Settlement
subtopics.summary: Several MC14 agendas remained contested. Dispute settlement reform seeks to restore a two-tier binding system, because the Appellate Body has been non-functional since 2019. Agriculture talks seek a permanent solution on public stockholding for food security, while fisheries talks target bans on harmful subsidies.
facts: Dispute settlement reform aims to restore a two-tier binding dispute system.
The Appellate Body has been non-functional since 2019.
Agriculture talks seek a permanent solution for public stockholding for food security.
The agriculture agenda also seeks to reduce trade-distorting subsidies and improve market access.
Market access is crucial for developing countries like India.
Developed countries remain reluctant to expand PSH flexibilities.
Fisheries talks aim to ban harmful subsidies causing overcapacity and overfishing.
Members agreed to continue negotiations on curbing subsidies for distant-water fishing fleets.
LDC graduation support includes transition mechanisms for trade benefits.
The future roadmap aims to finalise outcomes by MC15.

subtopics.title: Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD)
subtopics.summary: The IFD Agreement is a plurilateral pact, binding only on its signatories, that aims to make investment procedures transparent, efficient and predictable. It was launched under a Joint Statement Initiative at MC11 in Buenos Aires in 2017 and finalised in 2023. India opposed bringing it into the WTO's multilateral framework, citing mandate, consensus, policy space and geopolitical concerns.
facts: The IFD Agreement is a plurilateral agreement, binding only on signatories.
It was launched under a Joint Statement Initiative at MC11, Buenos Aires, in 2017.
It was finalised in 2023.
The IFD Agreement is based on the Most-Favoured-Nation principle.
Its objective is to make investment procedures transparent, efficient and predictable.
It covers investment facilitation: procedures, approvals and transparency.
It excludes market access, investment protection, government procurement and investor-state dispute settlement.
Its firewall clause prevents IFD rules from overriding Bilateral Investment Treaties.
Its appeal mechanism requires independent tribunals for dispute review.
India's concerns: investment is not strictly a trade subject, JSIs seem to bypass consensus, binding rules may limit FDI regulation, and geopolitical concerns.

subtopics.title: IQAir report 2025: scope and compliance
subtopics.summary: The 8th World Air Quality Report 2025 was released by Swiss IQAir, which assesses air quality using PM2.5 concentrations. IQAir's coverage grew from 134 countries in 2023 to 143 countries and 9,446 cities in 2025. Only 14% of cities met the WHO PM2.5 annual guideline in 2025, down from 17% in 2024.
facts: Report: 8th World Air Quality Report 2025, by Swiss IQAir
IQAir assessments are based on PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) concentrations
Coverage: 134 countries in 2023, then 143 countries and 9,446 cities in 2025
Only 14% of cities complied with the WHO PM2.5 annual guideline in 2025
City compliance share declined from 17% in 2024
Only 13 countries/territories met the WHO PM2.5 guidelines
130 of 143 countries and territories failed to meet safe air quality standards
Nieuwoudtville (South Africa) recorded as World's Cleanest City, PM2.5 level 1.0 µg/m³
IQAir is a Swiss air quality technology company founded in 1963, HQ in Goldach, Switzerland

subtopics.title: Most polluted countries, cities and regions
subtopics.summary: Pakistan was the most polluted country in 2025, with PM2.5 levels over 13 times the WHO limit. Loni in Uttar Pradesh was the most polluted city, about 22 times above WHO guidelines. Five of the world's ten most polluted cities are in India, and Central and South Asia remain the most polluted regions globally.
facts: Most polluted country in 2025: Pakistan, PM2.5 at 67.3 µg/m³
Pakistan's PM2.5 level is over 13 times the WHO limit
Pakistan was followed by Bangladesh, Tajikistan, Chad and Democratic Republic of Congo
Most polluted city: Loni, Uttar Pradesh, about 22 times WHO guidelines
5 of the world's 10 most polluted cities are in India: Loni, Byrnihat, Delhi, Ghaziabad, Ula
India ranked 6th most polluted country in 2025 (5th in 2024)
New Delhi is the world's most polluted capital for 8 consecutive years
India accounted for 74 of the world's 100 most polluted cities in 2024
Central and South Asia remain the most polluted regions globally

subtopics.title: National framework and monitoring tools in India
subtopics.summary: India's National Air Quality Index, launched in 2014, explains pollution in simple categories. The Graded Response Action Plan is an emergency measure that applies only when air quality shifts from Poor to Very Poor, and the Supreme Court approved it in 2016. The National Clean Air Programme, launched in 2019, targets a 40% cut in average particulate matter by 2026 in 131 cities.
facts: National Air Quality Index (2014) communicates air quality in easy terms; launched by Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)
AQI categories: Good, Satisfactory, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor, Severe
GRAP (2017): emergency measures that kick in only when air quality shifts from Poor to Very Poor
GRAP was submitted by CPCB and approved by the Supreme Court in 2016 (MC Mehta vs Union of India)
GRAP is implemented by the Commission for Air Quality Management
National Clean Air Programme launched in 2019 by the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change
NCAP goal: 40% reduction in average particulate matter concentrations by 2026 in 131 cities
The 131 non-attainment cities under NCAP were identified by CPCB
PRANA portal launched to track NCAP progress and regulate air pollution in non-attainment cities
SAFAR is a Ministry of Earth Sciences initiative for city-wide and localised air quality monitoring

subtopics.title: Vehicle, fuel, farm and legal measures
subtopics.summary: Vehicle norms, clean-fuel schemes and farm tools target different sources of pollution. Bharat Stage VI became mandatory nationwide in 2020, while FAME promotes electric and hybrid vehicles. Legal protection includes the Fundamental Duty in Article 51A(g), added in 1976, and the reading of Article 21 to cover a healthy environment.
facts: Bharat Stage VI (2020): mandatory leap from BS-IV to BS-VI, implemented nationwide
FAME scheme promotes adoption of electric and hybrid vehicles
Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana provides LPG as clean cooking fuel, reducing biomass-based cooking
SATAT initiative promotes compressed bio-gas to manage agricultural waste
GRIHA encourages sustainable, eco-friendly practices in building construction and operation
Turbo Happy Seeder uproots stubble and sows seeds in the cleared area
Pusa Bio-Decomposer turns crop residue into manure in 15-20 days; developed by Indian Agricultural Research Institute
42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Clause (g) in Article 51A: protecting and improving the natural environment is a Fundamental Duty
Article 21 interpreted to include the right to a healthy environment
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; Environment Protection Act, 1986

chapters.title: Science and Technology, Defence and Space

subtopics.title: Criticality and neutron balance
subtopics.summary: A reactor reaches criticality when its nuclear fission chain reaction becomes self-sustaining, and this depends on the balance of the neutron population in the core. The multiplication factor k compares the neutrons in one generation with the previous generation. The value of k decides whether a reactor is subcritical, critical or supercritical.
facts: Criticality: the state in which the nuclear fission chain reaction is self-sustaining.
Depends on the neutron population balance in the reactor core.
Multiplication factor k: neutrons in one generation divided by neutrons in the previous generation.
Subcritical (k < 1): neutron population decreases and the chain reaction dies out.
Critical (k = 1): neutron population remains constant and the reaction is steady and self-sustaining.
Supercritical (k > 1): neutron population increases exponentially and power output rises rapidly.
The PFBR achieved its first criticality, marking entry into Stage II of the nuclear programme.

subtopics.title: PFBR design and breeding
subtopics.summary: The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor uses Mixed Oxide fuel derived from reprocessed spent fuel. Its core is surrounded by a Uranium-238 blanket in which fast neutrons convert U-238 into Plutonium-239. Liquid sodium is the coolant, and the reactor has a capacity of 500 MWe.
facts: Fuel: Mixed Oxide (MOX) of plutonium and uranium.
The MOX fuel is derived from reprocessed spent fuel.
The core is surrounded by a Uranium-238 blanket, called the breeder blanket.
The breeder mechanism converts U-238 into Plutonium-239.
Uses fast neutrons to produce more nuclear fuel than it consumes while generating power.
Coolant system uses liquid sodium.
Liquid sodium has high thermal conductivity and does not slow neutrons.
Type: Fast Breeder Reactor with a capacity of 500 MWe.

subtopics.title: Benefits: fuel, waste and energy
subtopics.summary: The PFBR produces more fuel than it consumes, which extends the use of nuclear resources. It recycles spent fuel from Stage I reactors, which reduces the volume of nuclear waste and its long-term radiotoxicity. The booklet also says it extracts about 60 times more energy from natural uranium than traditional PHWRs.
facts: Result: the PFBR produces more fuel than it consumes.
Waste reduction: recycles spent fuel from Stage I reactors.
Reduces the volume of nuclear waste.
Reduces long-term radiotoxicity of nuclear waste.
Energy efficiency: extracts about 60 times more energy from natural uranium than traditional PHWRs.
PHWR stands for Pressurized Heavy Water Reactor, the comparison point for energy efficiency.

subtopics.title: India's three-stage nuclear programme
subtopics.summary: India's three-stage nuclear power programme was formulated by Homi Jehangir Bhabha to achieve long-term energy security using uranium and thorium resources. Stage I uses PHWRs, Stage II uses fast breeder reactors with MOX fuel and liquid sodium, and Stage III uses thorium-based advanced reactors. India presently has 24 nuclear power reactors operating in 6 states.
facts: Formulated by Homi Jehangir Bhabha.
Aim: long-term energy security using uranium and thorium resources.
Stage I: PHWR with natural uranium fuel, heavy water coolant and heavy water moderator.
Stage I breeds Plutonium-239.
Stage II: Fast Breeder Reactor using MOX (Pu-239 + U-238) fuel and liquid sodium coolant.
Stage III: Advanced HWR / Thermal Breeder using Uranium-233 derived from thorium.
Stage III uses light water as coolant and heavy water as moderator.
India presently has 24 nuclear power reactors operating in 6 states, with installed capacity of 8780 MWe.
Kudankulam Power Plant in Tamil Nadu is the newest and largest; Tarapur Power Plant in Maharashtra is the first and oldest.
Atomic Energy Act, 1962 governs nuclear facilities; the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) regulates them.

topics.title: INS Aridaman: India's Third Nuclear-Powered Ballistic Missile Submarine

subtopics.title: INS Aridaman and SSBN Features
subtopics.summary: India commissioned INS Aridaman, its third nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine, which marks a milestone of 3 operational SSBNs at sea. It is an indigenous Arihant-class SSBN powered by an 83 MW Pressurised Compact Light-Water Reactor. The booklet describes it as equipped with 8 vertical launch systems and as carrying K-4 missiles with a 3,500 km range. SSBNs are typically the largest and most complex type of nuclear-powered submarine.
facts: INS Aridaman is India's 3rd nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN).
Its commissioning marks a milestone of 3 operational SSBNs at sea.
It is the 3rd indigenous Arihant-class SSBN, after INS Arihant and INS Arighaat.
Powered by an 83 MW Pressurised Compact Light-Water Reactor.
Equipped with 8 vertical launch systems.
Firepower: K-4 missiles with 3,500 km range, plus capability to carry more K-15 missiles.
Built at the Ship Building Centre, Visakhapatnam, under the ATV programme.
Benefits: stealth (low noise), extended submerged operations and improved survivability.
SSBN stands for Ship Submersible Ballistic Nuclear; it can carry ballistic missiles that may be nuclear armed.

subtopics.title: Arihant-Class Submarines
subtopics.summary: The booklet shows the Arihant class with three submarines: INS Arihant (commissioned 2016), INS Arighaat (commissioned 2024) and INS Aridaman. INS Arighaat is similar to Arihant in power, launch tubes and displacement but much more technologically advanced. The specifications of Arihant-class submarines are classified, so the booklet's sketch is only an approximation. Nuclear submarines are grouped into SSN, SSGN and SSBN types, each with a different weapons role.
facts: The Arihant-class comparison covers three submarines: INS Arihant, INS Arighaat and INS Aridaman.
INS Arihant was commissioned in 2016; its firepower is K-15 Sagarika missiles.
INS Arighaat was commissioned in 2024.
INS Arighaat is similar to Arihant in power, launch tubes and displacement, but much more technologically advanced.
Specifications of Arihant-class submarines are classified; the sketch is an approximation.
SSN (Submersible Ship Nuclear) carries conventional weapons.
SSGN (Ship Submersible Guided Nuclear) carries guided missiles with conventional warheads.
SSBN is typically the largest and most complex type of nuclear-powered submarine.

subtopics.title: Strategic Significance for India
subtopics.summary: INS Aridaman completes India's nuclear triad, which enables nuclear delivery from land, air and sea. Its second-strike capability provides assured retaliation and supports the No First Use doctrine. The booklet says the submarine improves strategic reach in the Indian Ocean Region and Indo-Pacific and boosts Credible Minimum Deterrence. India is placed among the countries with operational nuclear triads, which the booklet lists as USA, Russia, UK, China and France.
facts: Completes India's nuclear triad, enabling nuclear delivery via land, air and sea.
Provides second-strike capability, meaning assured retaliation capability.
Supports India's No First Use doctrine.
Improves strategic reach in the Indian Ocean Region and Indo-Pacific.
Boosts Credible Minimum Deterrence.
Places India among countries with operational nuclear triads.
Other countries with operational nuclear triads listed: USA, Russia, UK, China, France.

subtopics.title: Submarine Building Programmes
subtopics.summary: The 30-year Submarine Building Plan was approved by the Cabinet Committee on Security in 1999, after the Kargil War, and aimed to build 24 conventional submarines indigenously by 2030. Under Project 75, six Kalvari-class diesel-electric submarines were being built at Mazagon Dock Limited, and INS Kalvari was commissioned in 2017. Project 75I, approved in 2007 as Phase II, is the first project under the Strategic Partnership Model. Project 751 adds AIP technology, which lets submarines stay submerged for up to 2 weeks.
facts: After the Kargil War (1999), the Cabinet Committee on Security approved a 30-year Submarine Building Plan.
The plan included building 24 conventional submarines indigenously by 2030.
Project 75 is Phase I (2000-2015) of the Indian Navy's 30-year indigenous submarine plan.
Six Kalvari-class (Scorpene-based) diesel-electric attack submarines were being built at Mazagon Dock Limited.
INS Kalvari, the first Project 75 submarine, was commissioned in 2017.
Project 75I, approved in 2007 as Phase II, is the first project under the Strategic Partnership Model.
Project 75I aims to procure diesel-electric attack submarines with fuel cells and AIP.
Conventional diesel-electric submarines must surface every 48 hours to be recharged.
Project 751 uses AIP technology to build six submarines that can stay submerged for up to 2 weeks.
Five foreign OEMs: Daewoo (South Korea), Naval Group (France), Rosoboronexport (Russia), Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems (TKMS, Germany), Navantia (Spain).

topics.title: NASA's Artemis Programme and Space Missions

subtopics.title: Artemis Programme and the Artemis II Mission
subtopics.summary: NASA's Artemis Programme aims to land humans on the Moon and is named after the Moon Goddess of Greek mythology. It proceeds in stages, beginning with an unmanned Artemis I that launched the Orion spacecraft, followed by the crewed Artemis II lunar flyby and then Artemis III, which is to return humans to the Moon. A Lunar Gateway Station is planned as a docking point for astronauts and for scientific research.
facts: Artemis is named after the Moon Goddess in Greek mythology.
Objective: land humans on the Moon by 2025, including the first woman and the first person of colour.
Artemis I was an unmanned mission that began with the launch of the Orion spacecraft on the Space Launch System.
Artemis II is a crewed lunar flyby; astronauts travel around the Moon and return to Earth without landing.
Artemis II crew of four: Reid Wiseman (Commander), Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen.
Jeremy Hansen is the first Canadian and non-American to fly on a lunar mission.
Artemis II is expected to last about 10 days, following a free-return trajectory, and splash down in the Pacific Ocean.
Artemis II launch site: Kennedy Space Center, Florida, USA.
Artemis III aims to return humans to the Moon.
Lunar Gateway Station is planned for 2029, serving as a docking point and for scientific research.

subtopics.title: Artemis Accords
subtopics.summary: The Artemis Accords were announced by NASA in 2020 and were established by the US State Department and NASA together with seven other founding members. They set out common principles for the civil exploration and use of outer space, including the Moon, Mars, comets and asteroids, for peaceful purposes. The Accords build on the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 but are not legally binding.
facts: Announced by NASA in 2020.
Established by the US State Department and NASA with 7 other founding members.
Founding members include Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom.
A set of principles and guidelines for international cooperation in space exploration.
Purpose: common principles to govern civil exploration and use of outer space, the Moon, Mars, comets and asteroids, for peaceful purposes.
Builds upon the Outer Space Treaty of 1967.
Nature: not legally binding.
Members: 63 countries.
India joined in 2023 as the 27th member.
Russia and China are not part of the Artemis Accords.

subtopics.title: Human Spaceflight and Gaganyaan
subtopics.summary: Yuri Gagarin of the Soviet Union was the first human in space in 1961, and Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space in 1963. India's Gaganyaan Project will launch a three-person crew on a three-day mission to a 400 km orbit, which would make India the fourth nation to do so after the United States, Russia and China. Vyommitra and the SAKHI app support the programme, with Vyommitra flying ahead of Gaganyaan and SAKHI supporting crew health and communication.
facts: Yuri Gagarin, Soviet cosmonaut, was the first human in space (Vostok, 12 April 1961).
Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman to enter space (1963).
Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian in space (Soyuz T-11, 3 April 1984).
Shubhanshu Shukla was the second Indian in space and the first on the ISS (Axiom-4, 2025).
Gaganyaan is India's first human spaceflight programme, with a three-person crew on a three-day mission to a 400 km orbit.
Gaganyaan would make India the 4th nation to launch humans after the United States, Russia and China.
Out of 4 astronaut designates (Vyomnauts), 3 will be selected for the final mission.
Gaganyaan comprises a crew module and a service module; developed by ISRO and launched on GSLV Mk III (LVM3).
Crew training takes place at the Human Space Flight Centre, Bengaluru.
Vyommitra is a woman robot astronaut (half humanoid) that will fly ahead of Gaganyaan; the name means Space-Friend.

subtopics.title: Lunar Missions: Chandrayaan and Moon Landings
subtopics.summary: India's Chandrayaan-1, launched in 2008, mapped the Moon's surface in unprecedented detail and found water ice in polar craters. Chandrayaan-3, launched in 2023, made India the first nation to soft-land on the lunar South Pole. Chandrayaan-4 is slated for 2028 to bring rock samples back to Earth, and Chandrayaan-5 is a joint mission of ISRO and JAXA to explore the Moon for water and other resources.
facts: Chandrayaan-1 (2008) was India's first lunar mission.
Chandrayaan-1 mapped the Moon's surface in unprecedented detail, discovering water ice in polar craters.
Chandrayaan-2 (2019) carried an orbiter, the Vikram lander and the Pragyan (Wisdom) rover.
Chandrayaan-3 (2023) was a second attempt after Chandrayaan-2, using GSLV Mk III.
With Chandrayaan-3, India became the first nation to soft-land on the lunar South Pole.
With Chandrayaan-3, India became the 4th nation to soft-land anywhere on the Moon.
Chandrayaan-4 is slated for launch in 2028 and aims to bring lunar rock samples back to Earth.
Chandrayaan-5 (Lunar Polar Exploration, LUPAX) is a joint initiative of ISRO and JAXA.
Landing on the Moon: Soviet Union first (Luna 9, 1966), United States second (Apollo, 1969), China third (Chang'e, 2013).
Japan became the 5th nation to land on the Moon (SLIM, 2024).

topics.title: R. Vaishali's FIDE Women's Candidates Win 2026

subtopics.title: Vaishali's Candidates win
subtopics.summary: R. Vaishali won the FIDE Women's Candidates Tournament 2026 in Nicosia, Cyprus, by defeating Kateryna Lagno of Russia in the final round. She finished with 8.5 out of 14 points and became the first Indian woman to claim the Candidates title. Her next challenge is the Women's World Chess Championship against Ju Wenjun of China, later in 2026.
facts: Event: FIDE Women's Candidates Tournament 2026
Venue: Nicosia, Cyprus
Final round: defeated Kateryna Lagno (Russia) to clinch the title
Final score: 8.5 out of 14 points
Milestone: first Indian woman to claim the Candidates title
Next challenge: reigning champion Ju Wenjun (China)
Women's World Chess Championship challenge due later in 2026

subtopics.title: India's world titles and milestones
subtopics.summary: Indian players hold several major chess titles. Viswanathan Anand won the FIDE World Chess Championship five times, and Gukesh Dommaraju became world champion in 2024 as the second Indian to win the title. Divya Deshmukh and Pranav Venkatesh added to India's record in 2025, and Koneru Humpy has a 2019 world rapid title.
facts: Viswanathan Anand won the FIDE World Chess Championship in 2000, 2007, 2008, 2010 and 2012
Gukesh Dommaraju won the FIDE World Chess Championship 2024, held in Singapore
Gukesh defeated Ding Liren (China) to become world champion
Gukesh is the 2nd Indian to win the FIDE World Chess Championship, after Anand
Gukesh is the 18th World Chess Champion in history
Divya Deshmukh won the FIDE Women's World Cup 2025 in Batumi, Georgia
Divya defeated Koneru Humpy in the Women's World Cup 2025 final
Pranav Venkatesh won the FIDE World Junior Chess Championship 2025 in Montenegro

Koneru Humpy clinched the Women's World Rapid Chess Championship title in 2019

subtopics.title: FIDE, the global chess body
subtopics.summary: FIDE (Fédération Internationale des Échecs), the International Chess Federation, is the global governing authority for chess. Founded in Paris in 1924, it oversees major international competitions and sets rules and rating standards. Its headquarters is in Lausanne, Switzerland, and Arkady Dvorkovich is its President.
facts: Full name: Fédération Internationale des Échecs (International Chess Federation)
Established in Paris in 1924
Headquarters: Lausanne, Switzerland
Serves as the global governing authority for chess
Oversees all major international competitions
Sets rules and rating standards
President: Arkady Dvorkovich

quizzes.title: VP Visit: Ties and Schemes
quizzes.passage: Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan made the first-ever bilateral visit to Sri Lanka and held talks with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in Colombo. The visit highlighted several areas where India and Sri Lanka work together. India has been Sri Lanka's largest trade partner and largest source of tourists, and the two countries signed a free trade agreement in 2000. Cooperation also extends to development projects, including the construction of a solar power plant at Sampur in Sri Lanka. Defence ties are expressed through joint exercises between the armed forces, such as SLINEX, MITRA SHAKTI and MILAN. The visit also brought the Overseas Citizen of India scheme into focus. During this period Sri Lanka joined the International Big Cat Alliance. The two neighbours are separated by the Palk Strait, and the uninhabited island of Katchatheevu lies in that strait. Regional forums such as BIMSTEC and SAARC also feature in the India-Sri Lanka relationship. Sri Lanka's President is Anura Kumara Dissanayake, while its Prime Minister is Harini Amarasuriya. Together, trade, development, defence, diaspora and regional cooperation form the main dimensions of the bilateral relationship discussed during the visit.

quizzes.title: Katchatheevu: Claims and Agreements
quizzes.passage: Katchatheevu is a small island located in the Palk Strait between India and Sri Lanka. The island is uninhabited, yet its ownership remained a point of dispute between the two countries for a long time. Sri Lanka's claim rests on history, since the island was initially ruled by a kingdom of Sri Lanka in the early medieval period. Sri Lanka also argues that a European power which occupied the island for over a century exercised jurisdiction over the islet. India's claim, on the other hand, holds that control of the island later passed to a zamindari, which functioned under a ruling dynasty. Over the years, maritime agreements tried to settle the dispute and strengthen ties. One agreement allowed Indian fishermen continued access to the island, and a later additional agreement prevented both countries from fishing in each other's exclusive economic zones. After the civil war in Sri Lanka ended, tensions rose over Indian fishermen in Sri Lankan waters, leading to arrests, torture allegations and renewed demands over the island.

quizzes.title: Bill and Lok Sabha expansion: practice MCQs
quizzes.passage: In April 2026, the government proposed the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 along with a Delimitation Bill, 2026. Delimitation is the process of redrawing constituency boundaries so that each constituency has a roughly equal population and representation keeps pace with population change. For the Lok Sabha, the proposal is to change the number of seats and to decide which census should serve as the population base for allocating them. Because population growth has been uneven across regions, a fresh allocation could shift the share of seats held by different states. States that grew faster could gain seats, while states with slower population growth could see their share fall. The Bill is also linked to women's reservation, which an earlier law set out but tied to the completion of a census and a delimitation exercise. Supporters say the Bill would bring the House closer to a fair and representative structure. Critics argue that the choice of population data and the discretion given to Parliament could weaken federal balance and invite political influence over boundary-making. The debate therefore centres on how the House should grow, which data should count, and who should control the process.

quizzes.title: Women's reservation: practice TITA

quizzes.title: Phase I digital census practice set

Digital technology runs through the process, and a self-enumeration option allows citizens to provide their own census details. Population counting has a long history in India. Ancient texts such as the Arthashastra, the Ain-e-Akbari and the Rig Veda mention population counts. The modern census is supported by law. The Census Act, 1948 provides the legal mandate and makes participation mandatory, and the Union has the power to conduct the census under the Constitution. The work is managed by the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India. Since Independence, India has held several censuses. Unlike sample surveys, the census offers comprehensive population data, which is useful for planning healthcare, education and infrastructure. The data also helps track changes in population over time. The census also supports progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals with robust data on health, education and poverty indicators. Phase I therefore builds on a long record of counting while bringing new digital methods to the process.

quizzes.title: Caste and census history typed answers
quizzes.passage: Counting people has a long history in India, and ancient texts such as the Arthashastra refer to population counts. It is the only one in the modern series to show a decline in population across a decade, which makes it a notable point in demographic history. Since Independence, the country has conducted repeated censuses, and each has added to the record of how the population has changed over time. Many tribal families also resent laws that limit their access to forest resources. quizzes.title: Decline and Response Check
quizzes.passage: In recent years, the number of districts affected by Left Wing Extremism has fallen sharply, and violence has declined in step. Security forces have moved into areas that were once hard to reach. Specialised units operating from bases closer to remote zones have pressed the movement hard, while the state has also tried to close the gap between remote regions and the rest of the country. Connectivity has played a major role. Better road links have reduced the geographical isolation in which insurgents once moved, and expanded mobile networks have helped counter propaganda and bring tribal regions into the digital world. Investigation agencies have carried out operations and seized assets, which has disrupted the networks that supply funds from urban areas. The movement also had a parallel system of governance of its own. Administrative efforts have aimed to replace that system with state institutions, including residential schools and programmes for aspirational districts. quizzes.title: Gujarat UCC Provisions Check
quizzes.passage: Gujarat has passed the Uniform Civil Code Bill 2026, and with this step it has become the second state to enact a Uniform Civil Code. The idea behind such a code is that the laws on marriage, divorce and inheritance should be the same for all citizens, irrespective of their religious affiliation, instead of being governed by separate religious personal laws. The Gujarat code creates one civil framework for these areas. It places strong emphasis on gender equality and aims to remove discriminatory practices against women. The code also brings in mandatory registration requirements for both marriages and live-in relationships, and it lays down a formal process for separations. Personal laws have long been a sensitive matter in India because many civil laws are closely linked with religious beliefs. For this reason, the code makes room for certain exceptions. Communities whose customary practices and cultural identity need to be preserved are kept outside its scope. Goa has followed a form of common civil code for a long time, and it is often cited as an example of how such a code can work in practice. Uttarakhand, which came before Gujarat, was the first state to adopt such a code after pre-Independence Goa.

quizzes.title: Courts and Views on UCC
quizzes.passage:
Indian courts have often been asked to decide whether personal laws can override individual rights. In one landmark case, the Supreme Court held that a Muslim woman could continue to claim maintenance from her husband under the criminal procedure law even after the period of waiting that follows divorce had ended. In a later case, the Court declared a form of instant divorce practised among Muslims unconstitutional, holding that it violated the dignity and equality of Muslim women, and it suggested that Parliament should frame a law to regulate Muslim marriages and divorces. Another judgment held that personal and customary laws must be tested against the fundamental rights, and that no religious practice can claim supremacy over the Constitution. The Supreme Court has also praised a state where a common civil code is already in force as a shining example for the country.

The views of other institutions have differed as well. A Law Commission in 2018 found that a uniform code was neither necessary nor desirable at that stage, and it recommended reforming family laws across religions instead. The Central Government, by contrast, favours a uniform code. Later, a fresh Law Commission issued a notification inviting public views on the subject. The framers of the Constitution did not intend total uniformity, which is why personal laws were placed in a list under which both Parliament and state legislatures can make laws.

quizzes.passage: The Mahanadi water dispute is a conflict between Odisha and Chhattisgarh over how the river's waters should be shared. Odisha, the downstream state, says that extensive upstream constructions in Chhattisgarh have reduced the water flowing into its territory. In Odisha's view, this decline threatens irrigation, drinking water supply, fisheries and the ecological sustainability of the state. Chhattisgarh, the upstream state, argues that it has a legitimate right to utilise river waters. It points out that it accounts for a larger share of the basin's catchment area. It also says its projects are necessary for regional development and water security. The conflict is most sharp during the non-monsoon season, when water availability downstream becomes critically important. A central obstacle is that the two states have no formal water-sharing agreement between them. The dispute grew more serious after upstream infrastructure work expanded, and Odisha took the matter forward by approaching the highest court of the country. Efforts at negotiation have so far not produced a shared formula. Both states continue to hold firmly to their positions, and the question of how the water should be divided remains open.

quizzes.title: 73rd Amendment: framework and provisions
quizzes.passage: Grassroots democracy in India received a major constitutional boost when a bill to amend the Constitution was introduced in the Lok Sabha in 1991. The aim was to bring governance closer to the people by giving local bodies a clear and permanent place in the Constitution. The amendment added a new part dealing with panchayats and laid down a common framework that States were expected to follow. Among its provisions are rules on how members and chairpersons are chosen, how seats are reserved for weaker sections and women, and how long a panchayat may function before fresh elections must be held. It also assigned the supervision of panchayat elections to a dedicated authority and required a body to review the finances of panchayats at regular intervals. Certain regions were kept outside this framework because of their special social and administrative character, and separate laws were made for some tribal areas. The rules were also extended to Union Territories, with the President empowered to specify exceptions. Local bodies were also expected to plan development for their own areas, which encouraged a bottom-up approach to planning. Regular elections became a central feature of local government under the new framework. The amendment was implemented in stages, and its adoption by individual States showed how a national framework could be translated into local practice across a federal country.

quizzes.title: Panchayati Raj committees
quizzes.passage: Rural development in India was shaped in the early 1950s by two government efforts, the Community Development Programme and the National Extension Service. Their performance needed a closer look, so the government set up a committee to examine how they were working and to suggest measures for their better functioning. Its most important proposal was a scheme of democratic decentralisation. This scheme later came to be known as Panchayati Raj. The idea was first put into practice in one State before other States followed. Over the following decades, more committees reviewed how these institutions were functioning. Some studied the administrative arrangements behind rural programmes, while others examined whether panchayats should be recognised and protected in the Constitution. Each report reflected a continuing effort to make local governance more effective. Panchayati Raj thus became a subject of national discussion, not just of local administration. A later constitutional amendment gave panchayats a fixed place in the Constitution, turning them from an experiment into a permanent feature of Indian governance. The journey of Panchayati Raj therefore shows how policy ideas, early trials and expert reports together shaped a system of grassroots democracy.

quizzes.title: Monetary Policy Committee Check
quizzes.passage: The Monetary Policy Committee is the body that sets the benchmark policy rate of the Reserve Bank of India, known as the Repo Rate. Its central purpose is to keep inflation within a specified target level, so that prices remain stable while the economy grows. The committee was created as a statutory body, and the central government holds the power to set up its composition. Its meetings are not occasional events, since the committee comes together regularly through the year to review the economic situation. Recently, the committee faced a difficult environment. Rising geopolitical tensions in West Asia increased global uncertainty, with volatile energy prices and disrupted trade flows. India was also experiencing a supply-side shock that raised input costs without necessarily reflecting excess domestic demand. Retail inflation stayed within the mandated band, and core inflation remained stable, which reduced the urgency for tightening. Trade agreements with several major partners were expected to boost exports and investment over the medium term. After weighing these factors, the committee chose to keep the Repo Rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent. The chosen stance was cautious and steady, in line with the goal of price stability. Such decisions shape borrowing costs for banks, businesses and households across the country, and they are closely followed by investors and students of the economy alike.

quizzes.title: Tools of the Central Bank
quizzes.passage: Monetary policy works through a set of instruments that the central bank can adjust to influence borrowing, spending and investment. The most closely watched of these is the Repo Rate, which sets the cost at which banks borrow from the central bank when they face a short-term shortage of cash. The Reverse Repo Rate moves in the other direction, since it is the rate at which the central bank borrows from banks. Changes in these rates affect loan prices across the economy. When rates rise, businesses and households face costlier loans, and demand slows. When rates fall, borrowing becomes cheaper and spending tends to pick up. Central banks, however, do not rely on one tool alone. They also set rules on how much money banks must hold, buy and sell securities in the market, and provide special windows for banks that need overnight funds. Careful use of the instruments helps keep prices stable while supporting a healthy pace of economic expansion.
