quizzes.title: MC14 and WTO Basics Quiz
quizzes.passage: The fourteenth Ministerial Conference of the World Trade Organization, known as MC14, was held in Yaoundé, Cameroon. The meeting ended without consensus, leaving several contentious issues unresolved. Members were divided over the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, and over agriculture and transparency norms. Because no agreement was reached, the pending issues were passed on to the WTO General Council, which meets in Geneva. The WTO is an intergovernmental organisation that manages and encourages international trade. It succeeded the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and was built on the results of the Uruguay Round negotiations. Its member countries work through several bodies, which share the work of running the organisation and handling trade disputes. Trade ministers and senior officials attend its main gatherings, and the organisation maintains strong relations with the United Nations. Trade disputes form a major part of the WTO's work, and the system for resolving them has been under strain. Members have been debating how to restore a binding system with two tiers. They have also discussed a permanent solution for public stockholding for food security, a demand that India and African nations have repeatedly raised. Fisheries subsidies and support for countries losing Least Developed Country status were also on the agenda.

quizzes.title: Digital Trade Recall
quizzes.passage: Digital trade became one of the most debated areas at the recent WTO Ministerial Conference. For a long time, members had kept a standing commitment that stopped them from taxing electronic transmissions. That commitment ended at the conference because members could not agree to renew it, so the question of taxing digital goods and services is now open. The outcome also reflected a deep North-South divide among members on several issues. Some members have chosen a different route. A group of members has advanced talks on a plurilateral agreement on electronic commerce. The proposed agreement focuses on areas such as data flows, digital transactions and consumer protection. These talks have moved forward even though the moratorium itself was not renewed. Digital goods and services cover a broad range of activities. Software, music, films and digital services all fall within the moratorium's coverage. The Appellate Body, which reviews decisions made by dispute panels, has also been part of the wider debate about how the WTO resolves disputes. Dispute settlement reform is one of the agenda items that members could not conclude at the conference.

quizzes.passage: Air quality around the world is often measured by the concentration of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5. Health agencies set a guideline for the annual average level of these particles, and a global assessment checks how many places meet it. The assessment discussed here is prepared by a technology company that measures air quality and reports the results. The findings are sobering. Only a small share of cities met the annual guideline in the latest year, and that share fell from the previous year. Most of the countries and territories assessed did not meet safe air quality standards. Only a handful of places met the guideline, and at least one city recorded very low particle levels, which shows that clean air is still possible.

quizzes.title: India's framework check
quizzes.passage: India manages air pollution through several tools that work at different stages. The first is a public information tool, a national index that converts complex pollution readings into simple categories from good to severe, so that citizens can understand the air they breathe. The second is an emergency framework. Its measures are triggered only when air quality worsens from one stage to a more dangerous one, and their purpose is to prevent further deterioration. The Supreme Court approved this emergency framework in a case concerning the environment. The third is a long-term national programme. It asks cities identified as non-attainment to reduce average particulate levels within a fixed period, and an online portal supports the tracking of its progress. The fourth is a monitoring initiative run by a government ministry, which provides city-wide and localised air quality information for major metropolitan areas and also issues weather forecasts and research. Each tool serves a different purpose, and none of them works alone. Public categories help people judge how careful to be on bad days, while emergency steps are reserved for the most severe deterioration. Long-term programmes address pollution that persists over many months and years, and monitoring tells authorities where action is needed. Together, these tools link public information, emergency response and long-term planning.

quizzes.title: Criticality and reactor choices
quizzes.passage:
A nuclear reactor produces useful power only when its chain reaction keeps going on its own. Whether this happens depends on the neutrons inside the core, because each fission releases neutrons that can trigger further fissions. Engineers track how many neutrons are produced in each round compared with the round before. If this ratio falls below the level needed, the reaction fades away. If it holds at that level, the power stays steady. If it climbs above, the output grows quickly and must be brought under control.

India's nuclear programme is designed to make the most of its resources over a long period. Early reactors use the fuel the country can readily supply, while later designs aim to create more fuel than they consume. The prototype reactor at Kalpakkam is a test of one such design, and its progress is being followed closely by scientists and policymakers.

Building a reactor that breeds fuel is demanding. Its core must be surrounded by material that captures neutrons and turns into new fuel. Its coolant must remove heat efficiently and be chosen with care, because the choice affects how the neutrons behave. These decisions shape the reactor's cost, its safety record and the amount of waste it leaves behind.

Regulation also matters. Nuclear and radiation facilities must follow national rules, and an expert body oversees their activities so that they run in a controlled way.

quizzes.title: India's energy programme
quizzes.passage:
Energy security has become a central goal for any country that depends on imported fuel. Nuclear power is one tool for this goal, because a small amount of fuel can produce a large amount of electricity. Its expansion also raises questions about waste, safety and the long-term supply of raw material. Planners have therefore looked for ways to close the fuel cycle, so that used fuel is recycled rather than simply stored. Such a plan also aims to reduce dependence on imports, which is why it attracts so much attention.

Such a plan works best when the programme is carefully staged. Each stage is meant to make better use of the country's resources than the one before it. Every stage brings its own engineering challenges, from choosing the moderator and coolant to designing the reactor core. Staging also gives engineers time to build skills and test new technology before the next step.

Nuclear facilities in the country must follow national rules and are checked by a regulator that oversees nuclear and radiation activities. The programme is described as supporting a clean, low-carbon energy transition. Progress is therefore measured not only in megawatts but also in less waste, more domestic fuel and the building of skills that place the country among the world's advanced nuclear nations.

quizzes.title: Aridaman Submarine Practice Set

Operators also value the ability to remain submerged for long periods and the improved survivability it offers. The submarine belongs to a family of Indian submarines that began with an earlier vessel and grew through later additions. Its construction was linked to a programme launched in the 1980s, which aimed to create an indigenous fleet of such submarines with Russian assistance. Several government bodies managed that programme, so the work drew on more than one organisation. The vessel also supports a sea-based leg of India's nuclear forces, alongside weapons delivered from land and from the air. Its role is tied to India's doctrine of not using nuclear weapons first and to the idea of a credible minimum deterrent. Readers preparing for examinations should note how these design goals, the programme history and the strategic role fit together. Taken as a whole, the vessel shows how India combines indigenous development with support from partners over several decades. Each of these points connects back to the submarine programme and the wider defence strategy.

quizzes.title: PIO and OCI Schemes: MCQ Practice
quizzes.passage:
Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) and Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) are two schemes that link people of Indian heritage living abroad with India. The OCI scheme was introduced through an amendment to the Citizenship Act, 1955. The PIO and OCI schemes were later merged into a single arrangement. The booklet presents the two categories side by side under the heading PIO VS OCI.

A foreign citizen can qualify as a PIO if a parent, grandparent or great-grandparent was born in India and was a permanent resident of India. The definition also covers a foreign citizen who is the spouse of a citizen of India or of a PIO, and it carves out exceptions for nationals of certain countries. PIO card holders enjoy parity with NRIs in economic, financial and educational benefits, and any future benefits given to NRIs are also available to PIO card holders.

OCI registration is open to certain foreign nationals with links to India, and minor children of such persons are also eligible. Registered OCI holders receive a multipurpose, multiple-entry, lifelong visa. This visa allows the holder to visit India at any time, for any length of time and for any purpose.

quizzes.title: Delimitation and the Commission: Practice Quiz
quizzes.passage: Delimitation is the process of drawing the boundaries of territorial constituencies so that representation stays fair as population changes. Over time, some constituencies grow much larger than others, which means that a vote in one area can carry less weight than a vote in another. For this reason, boundaries are not drawn once and left alone. Each redrawing exercise is carried out by a body called a Delimitation Commission, which is set up for that purpose. Such Commissions have been created under several Acts passed over a period of decades. They have not been appointed after every census, and at certain points the seat allocation among States was frozen to protect States that had controlled their population growth. Later changes to the Constitution continued these freezes. The same principle of fair representation also applies to the division of constituencies for State Assemblies, which follows its own constitutional provisions. Because the freeze was tied to population counts, the timing of the next redrawing has become a central question in the present debate over expanding the Lok Sabha. The question is not only how many seats exist but also how they are spread across regions. This makes the process both technical and politically sensitive, since every change in boundaries affects the candidates and voters in each area.

quizzes.passage: The proposed expansion of the Lok Sabha has been debated mainly for its effects on different parts of the country. Supporters of the change argue that a larger House would bring elected representatives closer to the people they serve, making it easier for citizens to raise their problems and seek a response. Critics reply that the benefits are not shared evenly, because the new seat arrangement would affect States differently depending on how their populations have grown over time. The discussion has also drawn in committees, public commentary and political parties, each setting out its own view of the reform. Taken together, these views show a debate about how representation, federal balance and effective governance should be weighed against one another. Supporters present the Uniform Civil Code as a progressive goal, and the Gujarat Bill is part of that case. quizzes.passage:
The Mahanadi dispute between Odisha and Chhattisgarh concerns how the river's water is shared, especially in the non-monsoon season, when water flowing downstream becomes critically important. The absence of a formal inter-state water-sharing agreement has added to the conflict, and Odisha has argued that upstream construction in Chhattisgarh has reduced the flow reaching its own territory. Chhattisgarh, for its part, maintains that it has a legitimate right to use river waters and that its projects serve regional development.

Such disputes are handled through a separate arrangement. The Constitution provides for them, and the law built on it allows a tribunal to be set up when a dispute needs adjudication. The tribunal then issues its decision, and the matter is decided on the basis of available evidence and legal principles.

The Mahanadi tribunal has expressed concern about repeated adjournments and the lack of substantive progress in talks. It has observed that no concrete proposals have been placed on record, despite assurances of settlement efforts. The tribunal has therefore given both states a final opportunity to agree on a formula.

Other river disputes in the country have also been handled through tribunals, each set up for a particular river. Read together, these cases show that water sharing between states is governed by a special framework rather than by routine legal channels.

quizzes.passage: The Reserve Bank of India, which is the country's central bank, manages the financial system through several tools. One of the most watched is the Repo Rate, the rate that acts as the cost of money for the banking system. Changes to this rate travel through the economy. When the rate is set higher, banks face costlier loans, and interest rates for consumers and businesses rise as well. Spending and investment tend to slow in such a situation. When the rate is eased, borrowing becomes cheaper and the overall supply of money in the economy increases, which can help growth. The Monetary Policy Committee decides the rate, and its decisions are based on a majority vote. The Committee meets at least four times each year. In its most recent review, the Committee chose to keep the rate unchanged, as geopolitical tensions in West Asia raised uncertainty about energy prices and trade. Supply-side shocks from global energy and commodity markets can also raise prices without reflecting excess demand. The RBI's role in the financial system is wide, covering monetary authority, supervision of banks, banker to the government and custodian of reserves. The rate is one of several instruments that the RBI can use at different times, depending on conditions in the economy. The aim of policy is to balance price stability with support for economic growth.

quizzes.passage: Inflation targeting is a monetary policy framework in which the central bank aims to keep the inflation rate within a range that is defined in advance. In India, the framework has been shaped by committee recommendations and by government decisions taken over time. The target and the permitted band around it are not chosen by the RBI alone. The government sets them in consultation with the Reserve Bank, and the arrangement is reviewed on a regular cycle. The RBI, for its part, works to maintain price stability while promoting economic growth. It carries out several roles in the financial system, and its supervisory functions also cover the issue of bank licences. It acts as the monetary authority of the country and as a supervisor of commercial banks, and it issues and destroys currency notes. It also acts as banker to the government and as the manager of foreign exchange. Retail inflation is watched against a mandated band set under the framework. The RBI was set up after a commission recommended its establishment, and the British government passed the Act that created it. The RBI also serves as lender of last resort for commercial banks. Taken together, these responsibilities place the RBI at the centre of the country's money and banking system.

quizzes.title: PFBR fuel, blanket and coolant
quizzes.passage: The PFBR at Kalpakkam has achieved first criticality, a milestone that the booklet links with the start of a new phase in India's nuclear programme. Criticality is the state of a nuclear reactor in which the fission chain reaction is self-sustaining. Whether a reactor reaches this state depends on the balance of the neutron population in its core. The multiplication factor, written k, is the ratio of the number of neutrons in one generation to the number of neutrons in the previous generation. The booklet presents this under the heading Criticality in Nuclear Reactors and names three types of criticality, which are distinguished by the value of k. When k is less than 1, the reactor is subcritical: the neutron population decreases over time and the chain reaction dies out. When k equals 1, the reactor is critical: the neutron population remains constant and the chain reaction is steady and self-sustaining. When k is greater than 1, the reactor is supercritical: the neutron population increases exponentially and the power output rises rapidly. The achievement was reported in April 2026 in the booklet's current affairs section. The booklet then turns to the reactor's key technical features, which it lists in a separate section.

quizzes.passage: India's position in global economic rankings is measured using nominal GDP in US dollar terms. The figure depends on domestic output in rupees and on the exchange rate against the dollar, so a weaker rupee lowers the dollar value of GDP. A revision of GDP data with a new base year also changes the figures. Special Additional Excise Duty, or SAED, is a levy on petroleum products that the government adjusts when global crude prices move. It works as a windfall tax in times of price surges, and unlike the GST, its revenue is kept by the Centre. Climate policy is another area of activity. Countries submit self-defined climate action plans under the Paris framework, and these plans are reported regularly. Synthetic gases used in cooling and foam industries are being phased down under an international amendment to the Montreal Protocol. Air conditioners and refrigerators are among the uses of these synthetic gases. Host nations for the UN climate conference are chosen through regional rotation. The rules also require a formal proposal to the UNFCCC Secretariat before a country can be chosen. If no host emerges, the venue shifts to Bonn, the seat of the UNFCCC. Rankings also influence investor sentiment and global confidence.

quizzes.title: Health Cooperation and Subject Rankings
quizzes.passage: The booklet's health and nutrition block covers nutrition policy, BRICS health cooperation and higher-education rankings. A 15-day nationwide campaign aims to drive behavioural change and improve nutritional outcomes for women and children, and it is one of the nutrition measures in the block. Mission POSHAN 2.0 is also part of the nutrition agenda. Traditional medicine is part of the health agenda, and the booklet describes the promotion of traditional, complementary and integrative medicine. A BRICS Mental Health and Wellness Initiative aims to strengthen mental healthcare systems, raise awareness and reduce stigma. The BRICS Health Working Group is also part of this cooperation. In higher education, the booklet reports on subject-wise global rankings. These rankings consider academic and employer reputation, citations per paper, the H-Index and an international research network. Engineering and technology is one of the subject areas in these rankings. Indian institutions have also shown a shift beyond the long-standing dominance of STEM subjects, which the booklet reads as a new trend.
